paragraphs.text: Telling your day is a chain, not a list. One thing happens, then the next, and the listener follows the chain. German gives you two very cheap links for that chain. A time phrase opens the sentence: {{de:Morgens}} or {{de:Dann}} or {{de:Am Sonntag}} — and because that phrase is heavy, the verb jumps behind it.
Morgens trinke ich einen Kaffee und esse Müsli mit Obst. Dann gehe ich ins Büro.

In English the order feels natural anyway; in German you have to notice that {{de:Dann gehe ich ins Büro}} puts the verb second and the subject after it. Say the two sentences aloud before you build your own — the rhythm teaches the rule faster than the explanation does.

Now swap in your own details. Your partner's only job is to guess whether the day you described is a weekday or a weekend. If you say {{de:Ich gehe ins Büro}}, they will answer {{de:Das ist nicht am Wochenende!}}

items.german: Morgens trinke ich einen Kaffee und esse Müsli mit Obst.
items.english: In the morning I drink a coffee and eat muesli with fruit.
Then I go to the office.

items.german: Mein Samstag ist super: Ich frühstücke und ...
items.english: My Saturday is great: I have breakfast and ...
That is not on the weekend!

blocks.passage: Morgens trinke ich einen Kaffee. Dann gehe ich ins Büro.
blocks.explanationEnglish: Your partner is guessing whether this is a working day. Going to the office means it is not a weekend, so the guess {{de:Das ist nicht am Wochenende!}} is the only reply that continues the game — the other two ask about the time, which nobody mentioned.

concept.title: Wochentag oder Wochenende
concept.rule: A weekday routine uses places like the office; a weekend routine uses sleeping in, shopping and meeting friends. Your partner listens for those cues and guesses which one you described.
concept.exampleGerman: Am Wochenende schläft Kaan lange. — Das ist nicht am Wochenende!
concept.exampleEnglish: On the weekend Kaan sleeps in. — That is not on the weekend!
